column2: A thousand fish are caught, marked, and let go. A while later, a second net catches a thousand. Of those, a hundred are marked.
Now look at the fish no net ever touched.
There are about eight thousand one hundred of them. And we can say how sure we are.
Why not count one patch and scale up? This net covers one hundredth of the lake. Four hundred fifty-one fish, times a hundred, is forty-five thousand one hundred.
Try two other spots. Same answer?
Not even close. In the weeds, eighty-eight thousand. In open water, two thousand eight hundred.
The net knows it covered a hundredth of the water. It can't know what share of the fish that was.
In nineteen fifty, the probabilist William Feller put this puzzle in his famous textbook. Others had been using it for years, and his book never mentions them.
Feller marked his fish with red spots. Ours glow, so you can see them.
Read it one way first. Of the thousand marked fish, the second net caught a hundred. One in ten.
So the second net probably caught about one in ten of all the fish. It caught a thousand. A thousand is one tenth of how many?
Ten thousand. The marked fish measured our net for us. It searched about a tenth of the fish.
Read the same fact the other way. One fish in ten in the second catch is marked, so about one in ten in the lake is.
Marked times second catch, over caught twice. A thousand times a thousand, over a hundred. Ten thousand. Call it the soup guess.
Why should that work? How sure can we be? And when does it fail?
Think about tasting soup. Stir it, and one spoonful tells you how salty the whole pot is.
We built this lake, so we can peek. The fisher can't. We marked the first thousand near the dock, and let them go there.
Watch them swim. Will the marks stay bunched up near the dock?
The fish stay crowded where they like to be. But the marks spread out evenly among them.
Wherever the second net goes, about one fish in ten it catches is marked. The catch is a tiny copy of the lake's mix.
Zoom in. A crowded patch has fifty fish, five of them marked. A sparse one has ten, with one marked. Both are one in ten.
Mixing is what makes the table fair. Being marked becomes unrelated to where a fish swims, so the second net catches marked fish in their fair share.
That's what independent means here. The second net doesn't care which fish were caught before.
To see exactly why, shrink the lake. Twenty fish, five of them marked. Our net holds four.
Random means every group of four is equally likely. How many groups are there?

Twenty choices for the first fish, nineteen for the second, then eighteen, then seventeen. But the same four fish come out in twenty-four orders, four times three times two times one, and that's still one netful. So divide by twenty-four. Four thousand eight hundred forty-five.
Sort them by how many marked fish they hold. Which pile is biggest?
One marked fish. One in four, same as the lake. The soup again.

Take the pile with two marked fish. Ten ways to pick two of the five marked ones. For each, a hundred and five ways to pick two of the fifteen unmarked ones, like shirts and pants. One thousand fifty.
Divide every pile by all four thousand eight hundred forty-five, and you get the chances. About twenty-eight percent, forty-seven, twenty-two, three, and under one.
Mathematicians call it the hypergeometric distribution. If we know the lake, we know the chances of every catch. But we only know the catch.
A new lake, and we don't know its size. We marked ten, caught ten, and three were marked.
The soup guess first. Ten times ten, over three?
About thirty-three. Now check it properly. What's the smallest the lake could be? We've already seen seventeen different fish.
For each possible lake size, ask how likely it is to see exactly three marked. A lake of twenty, about eight percent. Thirty-three, about thirty-two percent. Sixty, about sixteen.
Now sweep through every size.
The curve peaks at thirty-three, just as the soup guess said. It's called the likelihood. Think of it as a score for each lake size. How likely our catch would be, if the lake were that size.

Add up every height, out to lakes as big as you like, and you get about sixteen and two thirds, not one. The lake has one size. These aren't chances that it's a certain size. They're scores for comparing guesses.
Here's every lake size and every possible count at once.
Cut across at one lake size. What do you get?
The chances from the netfuls. They add to one.
Cut along at our three, and you get the score curve. Its heights add to sixteen and two thirds. Same mountains, two questions.
Feller found the top score without drawing anything. Compare each lake size with the one just below it.

In our small lake, the step from thirty-two to thirty-three comes down to two numbers, five hundred twenty-nine against five hundred twenty-eight. The top one wins, so the score goes up. From thirty-three to thirty-four, it's five hundred seventy-six against five hundred seventy-eight, so it goes down.
So take the top minus the bottom, written with letters. Multiply it out. What survives?
Marked times second catch, minus caught twice times lake size. While that's positive, the score is still rising.
Now write it with the table's four cells. It becomes first catch only times second catch only, minus caught twice times the dark cell.
In the small lake, seven times seven, minus three times sixteen. One, same as before. Back to Feller's lake.
So start with a small dark cell and let it grow. Where does the climb stop?
In each column, the green part is what the second net caught. While the unmarked side's green share is bigger, the score keeps climbing.
A hundred times eight thousand one hundred is eight hundred ten thousand. So is nine hundred times nine hundred. The shares match, the line is straight, and the table balances.
A straight line is exactly what two independent catches look like. So the careful argument and the soup guess give the same answer, rounded down to a whole fish.
At Feller's numbers the line is perfectly straight at ten thousand, so lakes of nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine and ten thousand tie for the top score. Feller just says ten thousand.
Let's check this by cheating. Build a lake of exactly ten thousand fish, and run Feller's experiment on it ten thousand times.
Where do the counts of fish caught twice pile up?
In a bell around a hundred. Most land within about nine of it.

But the estimate divides by that count, and dividing bends things. Ninety caught twice gives about eleven thousand one hundred. A hundred and ten gives about nine thousand one hundred. Ten too few pushes harder than ten too many.
Ninety-five percent of the estimates land from about eighty-five hundred to just over twelve thousand. Their average is about ten thousand and eighty, a little high.
Two lines of code. Always check a simulation against something you can compute exactly.
With a smaller experiment it gets worse. In a lake of a thousand, mark fifty and catch fifty. How often does the second catch hold no marked fish at all?
About one time in fourteen. Then the soup guess divides by zero.

Chapman's fix is to add one to each count, and subtract one at the end, as if one imaginary fish had been caught both times. It never divides by zero, and once you expect four or more caught twice, it's nearly exact on average.
So far the lake was known, and we watched the estimates scatter. Now turn it around. We don't know the lake. Which sizes could plausibly have given us our hundred caught twice?

Only nineteen hundred fish? Then the second net scooped up all nine hundred unmarked fish and only a hundred of the thousand marked ones. The chance of that is about five in a one followed by four hundred thirty zeros.
A million fish? Then we'd expect to catch about one marked fish, not a hundred.
Even at the best size, catching exactly a hundred had only about a four percent chance. Is that a problem?
Flip a hundred coins. Exactly fifty heads happens only about eight percent of the time, yet it's the most likely count.
Now the careful range. For each lake size, ask whether a catch of a hundred would land in that lake's middle ninety-five percent. Keep the sizes where it would.
Build that range for each experiment, and it rings the true size at least ninety-five times in a hundred, whatever the true size is. Like a ring toss.

For Feller's catch it runs from about eighty-four hundred to about twelve thousand one hundred. Close to the range we watched when the lake was known, but a different question. There the lake was fixed and the catch moved. Here the catch is fixed and the lake moves.
What makes the range tight?
Mostly, more fish caught twice. Four times as many halves the range. Catching a big share of the lake helps a little, and catching all of it leaves no doubt.
Every failure breaks one rule. The second catch must carry the same share of marked fish as the lake. Then it's a fair copy.
Some fish are bold and easy to catch, both times. Will the estimate come out too big, or too small?

Too small. Bold fish get caught twice more than their share, so the dark cell shrinks. In our lake, where three fish in ten are three times as easy to catch, the estimate comes out around seventy-seven fifty.
Fish that learn to love the bait do the same. Fish that learn to avoid it push the estimate up.
Marks that wash off make marked fish look unmarked. That pushes it up too.
Two thousand newcomers between the catches dilute the marks. Then you've counted the lake as it is at the second catch.
What if three fish in ten die between the catches?
The estimate doesn't move. Death doesn't care about marks, so the rule still holds.
And if the marks never mix, everything depends on where you fish. Fish near the release site, and you'd say sixty-two fifty. Fish the far side, and you'd say twenty-five thousand.
Around eighteen hundred, the French mathematician Laplace used the same table to count France. Births were written down, so in our table, each newborn is a marked fish.

At his request, officials counted everyone in chosen towns across France. About two million people, with about seventy-two thousand births a year. That's one birth for every twenty-eight and a bit people. Taking France's births as a million a year, that's about twenty-eight point four million people.
It counts bugs too. Say two reviewers read the same code without comparing notes. One finds thirty bugs, the other twenty-four, and twelve are the same. How many are still hiding?
Thirty times twenty-four, over twelve, is sixty. They found forty-two, so about eighteen. But twelve is a small number caught twice. An honest range is forty-seven to ninety-four bugs in all.
Reviewers of different skill are fine. Bugs of different difficulty are not. Easy bugs swell the caught-twice cell and pull the estimate down, like the bold fish. So read sixty as probably too low.

And it has counted the dead. In the war in Kosovo, in nineteen ninety-nine, several lists named about four thousand four hundred different victims between them. The names shared between lists estimated about ten thousand four hundred killed. Years later, a name-by-name count found nine thousand seven hundred ninety, inside the estimate's range.
France, the bugs, Kosovo. What do they share?
Each is a table with one cell nobody can see, filled in by the cells we can.
